title: The Sage Ruler and the Small State
bigQuestion: What kind of ruler and what kind of state does the Daodejing describe, and is it a book about politics or about personal life?

story.title: Don't Stir the Fish
story.kicker: A cook explains to a governor why a small fish falls apart if you stir it too much.
paragraphs: This scene is a teaching story written for this course, built around one line of the Daodejing. A new governor has just taken office in a river town. He is eager. He sends out new orders every morning. By the end of the month the town clerks cannot keep up, and the farmers are confused.

One evening the governor walks into the kitchen, hungry and tired. The cook is frying tiny river fish in a wide pan. The governor reaches for the spatula to turn them. The cook gently stops his hand. "If you stir them," she says, "they break apart. Let the heat do its work."

The governor laughs and says she sounds like a book. She says she is quoting one. Chapter 60 of the Daodejing, in James Legge's 1891 translation, begins: "Governing a great state is like cooking small fish." Readers have taken it for centuries as advice not to meddle too much.

The next morning the governor sends out no new orders. He asks the clerks which old ones people actually need. The story is invented, but the question is real. Readers of the Daodejing have argued for two thousand years about how much a ruler should do.
story.think: What would "stirring too much" look like in a school, a team or a town? Is there ever a time when stirring is needed?

lessons.title: Four Kinds of Rulers
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing chapter 17 ranks rulers, placing highest the one the people hardly know is there.
reading: Chapter 17 gives a ranking. The best rulers, it says, are those the people barely know exist. Next come rulers the people love and praise. Next, rulers they fear. Last, rulers they despise. The chapter moves from rule that is almost invisible to rule that is hated.

The chapter ends with the people's voice. In Legge's translation: "Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'" The best ruler's success is that the people feel they did it themselves. The Chinese word is *ziran*, often glossed "so of itself" or naturalness.

Readers compare this with the Analects. Analects 2.1 praises a ruler whose virtue draws the people like the pole star. Chapter 17 places the loved and praised ruler only second. Some readers see a sharp difference between the books here. Others see two ways of saying that the best rule does not force.

words.d: "so of itself"; naturalness, things happening from their own nature
a list that puts things in order from best to worst
in the Daodejing, a ruler who follows the Dao and governs without forcing

lessons.title: Cooking Small Fish
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing chapter 60 compares governing a great state to cooking small fish, which break apart if handled too much.
reading: Chapter 60 opens with one of the book's best-known lines. Legge: "Governing a great state is like cooking small fish." Small fish are delicate. Turn them too often and they fall to pieces. For centuries readers have taken the line as advice against meddling.

This is an *aphorism*: a short, memorable saying that packs an idea into a few words. The Daodejing is full of them. Aphorisms travel well. Chapter 60's line has been quoted by modern political leaders, including a U.S. president in the 1980s, as an image of limited government.

The rest of chapter 60 is less often quoted. It goes on to speak of spirits and the Dao. It says that when a state is ruled by the Dao, spirits do no harm to the people. Religious Daoist readers attend to this part. Political readers often stop after the first line. A close reader reads the whole chapter.

words.d: a short, memorable saying that states an idea
getting involved where it is not needed and making things worse
a large kingdom; in the Daodejing, the realm a ruler governs

lessons.title: More Laws, More Thieves
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing chapter 57 says that more prohibitions and laws bring more poverty and more crime, and the sage does little so the people change on their own.
reading: Chapter 57 makes a list of causes and effects. The more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people become. The more sharp weapons, the more disorder. The more clever skills, the more strange things appear. The more laws are posted, the more thieves there are. Each line pairs a ruler's action with a bad result.

Then the sage speaks. In paraphrase: I do not act, and the people change by themselves. I love stillness, and the people become upright. I do not meddle, and the people grow rich. I have no desires, and the people become simple. This is wu wei, non-action, applied to government.

Chapter 57 invites comparison with Analects 2.3, which also doubts laws and punishments. But the two books offer different cures. The Analects offers virtue and li, ritual. The Daodejing often doubts ritual too, and offers stillness and fewer desires. Both books question rule by force, in different ways.

words.d: a rule that forbids something
non-action or acting without forcing; in chapter 57, a ruler who does not meddle
the link between an action and what it leads to

lessons.title: A Village Within Sight
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing chapter 80 pictures a small state with few people, content at home, who never need to visit their neighbors.
reading: Chapter 80 draws a picture of a small state with few people. They have tools but do not use them. They have boats and carriages but no reason to ride them. They have weapons but no need to show them. They enjoy their food, clothes, homes and customs. The chapter describes a whole way of life in a few lines.

The chapter ends with a famous image. The next state is so close its roosters and dogs can be heard. Yet the people grow old and die without going back and forth. Readers call this a *utopia*: a picture of an ideal society. Some readers find it peaceful. Others find it closed off.

Scholars debate whether chapter 80 is a real political plan or a picture meant to make readers question ambition and conquest. The Daodejing was written in a time of wars between states. Some readers see the small state as a quiet answer to that age. Others read it as a picture of a calm inner life.

words.d: a picture of an ideal society, which may or may not be meant as a real plan
being satisfied with what one has
the period of wars among Chinese states, c. 475–221 BCE

check.why: Many scholars date the text to the time of wars among states, c. 475–221 BCE.

lessons.title: Three Treasures
lessons.mainIdea: In Daodejing chapter 67 the speaker names three treasures: gentleness or compassion, economy, and not putting oneself first.
reading: Chapter 67 speaks in the first person. Legge: "But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others." "Economy" here means frugality, using little. "Taking precedence" means going first or ranking above others.

Translators choose different words for the first treasure. Legge writes "gentleness." Many others write "compassion" or "kindness," the love a mother has for a child. The chapter says gentleness brings courage, economy brings generosity, and not going first lets one lead. Each treasure turns into a strength.

Readers find a pattern here. Each treasure looks weak at first. Each turns out strong. That fits the book's love of paradox and of water. Religious Daoists have treated the three treasures as guides for conduct. Philosophical readers treat them as the ruler's virtues. The same list serves both.

words.d: the three qualities named in Daodejing 67: gentleness or compassion, economy, and not putting oneself first
using little and not wasting
going first or ranking above others

lessons.title: Counting the Ruling Chapters
lessons.mainIdea: Many Daodejing chapters speak about rulers and states, which is why some readers call it a book for kings.
reading: Readers who count find that a large share of the Daodejing mentions the sage, the ruler or the state. Chapter 3 talks about keeping the people's hearts empty and their bellies full. Chapter 17 ranks rulers. Chapters 57, 60 and 80 speak of states. The book often addresses someone who rules.

That is why some scholars call it a guide for rulers, like other political writings of the Warring States. Others notice that almost every line can also be read about a single life. "The sage" can mean a king, or anyone who follows the Dao. Both readings have long histories.

This is a matter of *audience*: who a text is written for. The audience shapes the meaning. A line about not meddling means one thing to a king and another to a parent. Close readers ask who the speaker seems to address in each chapter, and note where the answer is unclear.

words.d: the people a text is written for
the wise person of the Daodejing, who may be read as a ruler or anyone who follows the Dao
reading a text as advice about government and power

lessons.title: Legalist Readers
lessons.mainIdea: The Legalist thinker Han Feizi wrote chapters explaining the Laozi, reading its non-action as a tool for a strong ruler.
reading: Han Feizi, who died in 233 BCE, was the leading Legalist writer. Legalists stressed clear laws, rewards and punishments, and a strong ruler. It may seem surprising that such a writer would read the Daodejing. Yet the book called the Han Feizi includes two chapters devoted to explaining and illustrating the Laozi.

Han Feizi read the Dao's quiet as a ruler's hidden power. A ruler who shows no desires, he argued, cannot be manipulated by ministers. He sits still and lets the laws work. In this reading, wu wei becomes a technique of control. It is very different from the gentle ruler of chapter 17.

Scholars call this a case of *appropriation*: taking a text and using it for one's own purpose. Many Daoist readers reject the Legalist reading. Others note that the Daodejing's short lines can support it. The case shows how a text about gentleness can be read as a text about power.

words.d: an early Chinese school of thought stressing strict laws, rewards, punishments and a strong ruler
the leading Legalist writer (d. 233 BCE), and the book of his writings
taking a text or idea and using it for one's own purpose

lessons.title: Emperors and Temples
lessons.mainIdea: Some emperors honored the Daodejing and Laozi, and religious Daoists read its ruling chapters in their own way.
reading: Early Han dynasty rulers, in the 100s BCE, favored a mix of Laozi's teaching and ideas linked to the Yellow Emperor. Historians describe court figures such as Empress Dou as supporters. Later, the Tang dynasty emperors, whose family name was Li, honored Laozi, also said to be named Li, as their ancestor.

Tang emperors had the Daodejing studied and, at times, added to the state exams. Emperor Xuanzong, in the 700s, wrote his own commentary on it. For these readers, the ruling chapters were real advice for real government. They also honored Laozi with temples and titles.

Religious Daoists read the same chapters within their own practice. For them, ruling the state and caring for the body can mirror each other. Heshang Gong's commentary often reads "the state" as the body as well. This double reading, state and self, is one of the oldest ways the book has been read.

words.d: the Chinese dynasty of 618–907 CE, whose rulers honored Laozi
a book of notes explaining a classic, line by line
"the Old Man by the River"; name given to the author of an early Daodejing commentary

lessons.title: Political or Personal?
lessons.mainIdea: Readers still debate whether the Daodejing's ruling chapters are political advice, personal wisdom, or both.
reading: Take the line from chapter 60: governing is like cooking small fish. A political reader hears advice to leaders: do not over-regulate. A personal reader hears advice about any task: do not fuss. A religious Daoist reader may hear advice about caring for body and spirit. The words stay the same. The *frame* changes.

Modern readers add new frames. Some writers on business quote the book on leadership. Some thinkers who favor limited government quote chapter 57. Some environmental writers quote its praise of letting things be. Scholars sometimes worry these readings pull lines out of their setting.

A close reader can hold several frames at once. First, ask what the chapter says in its own words. Second, ask who it seems to address. Third, describe how different readers have used it. The Daodejing's short, open lines make this range of readings possible. That openness is part of why it has lasted.

words.d: the point of view or setting a reader brings to a text
make too many rules
an explanation of what a text means

lessons.title: Comparing the Two Classics on Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects and the Daodejing both doubt rule by force, but they disagree about ritual, praise and how much a ruler should do.
reading: Set the two books side by side. Analects 2.1: a ruler of virtue is like the pole star, which all stars turn toward. Analects 2.3: lead by virtue and li, not punishments. Daodejing 17: the best ruler is barely known. Daodejing 57: more laws bring more thieves. Both books doubt harsh law.

They differ on ritual and praise. The Analects values li as the shape of good conduct and wants a ruler to be a visible model. The Daodejing is often wary of ritual; chapter 38 calls ritual a thin form of loyalty. It prefers a ruler who is hardly seen.

Readers have handled this difference in many ways. Some see the two as rivals. Some Chinese thinkers treated them as complements, one for public life and one for private. The idea of the "three teachings," Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist, as parts of one whole became common in later China. The course names these views without ranking them.

words.d: something that completes or balances another
Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, often seen in later China as parts of one whole
a person others copy; in the Analects, the ruler as an example
